paras: The lynching of Dan Blakeney was the hanging of a Black farm hand near Lancaster, South Carolina, on August 8, 1882, by a body of men who took him from constables escorting him to jail. He had been accused of attempting to assault the twelve-year-old daughter of his employer the night before. The Charleston News and Courier's Lancaster correspondent, who saw the body, endorsed the killing, and a short wire version of his report ran in papers across the country.

According to the Lancaster correspondent, Blakeney worked as a farm hand for 'a prominent citizen' who lived fourteen miles east of Lancaster. On the night of Monday, August 7, he was said to have entered the room of his employer's twelve-year-old daughter, fled when her screams woke the household, and been pursued and captured. The correspondent wrote that he 'confessed everything', and the Charleston wire repeated that he confessed, but no account quotes him or names a witness to the confession.

A posse of constables set out with Blakeney for the county jail, but about two miles from Lancaster a 'body of good citizens' took him from them by force and hanged him from a tree. No participant was named, and no report says how many men took part or whether the constables resisted. Hearing of the lynching, the correspondent went out early on August 9 to a lonely spot about a mile and a half east of town, where he found the body hanging from a small white oak 'with his toes touching terra firma.'

The same dispatch reported that on August 8 another Black man had been lodged in the Lancaster jail, charged with the rape of a 'mulatto' girl, and that threats were being made to lynch him as well. The correspondent attributed these threats to 'the colored people', while wire versions said only that lynching was 'threatened' or 'feared', or that 'the people' threatened it.

No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution for Blakeney's death appears in the coverage, and no later report on the second prisoner was found. The correspondent closed by asserting that 'a just but terrible fate is the verdict of all, both white and colored', a claim no other source tests.

The story reached the national press through a Charleston dispatch of August 9 crediting a special to the News and Courier, printed on August 10 by the National Republican, the Richmond Dispatch, the New-York Tribune, the Salt Lake Herald and others. Headlines adopted the accusation as fact: the National Republican ran it as 'Lynching the Fiends', the Richmond Dispatch listed 'A Rape Fiend Lynched in South Carolina', and the Wood River Times headed it 'A Would-Be Ravisher Lynched.' Western and Midwestern papers carried it as a single line in telegraph roundups on August 10 and 11, often with garbled names such as 'Don Blagely' and 'Dave Blakely.'

South Carolina weeklies printed fuller versions a week later; the Fairfield News and Herald ran the correspondent's letter under 'Lynching in Lancaster', and the Union Times reprinted its body. The Pickens Sentinel added its own approval, 'He was rightly disposed of', while the Yorkville Enquirer and Keowee Courier gave brief notices.

Accounts differ on timing: the Lancaster letter puts the hanging on the night of August 8, the Charleston wire on the morning of August 8, and an August 10 Charleston dispatch and the Cheyenne Daily Leader imply August 9. The correspondent's visit to the body early on August 9 makes his account the strongest on date and place. Late digests misplaced the event, the Port Tobacco Times putting Lancaster Court-house in North Carolina and the Douglas Independent reporting an unnamed lynching 'in Charleston on the 9th.'

reader.title: Lynching of Dan Blakeney
bases: A body of men took Dan Blakeney from constables taking him to jail and hanged him from a tree on an accusation of attempted assault (A27, A34, A2).

The Lancaster correspondent reports that 'an engaged [enraged] body of good citizens' seized Blakeney from a posse of constables and hanged him, and every wire calls it a lynching for an alleged attempted assault on a white girl (A27, A34, A3, A2).

Every detailed report traces to one Lancaster correspondent of the Charleston News and Courier, printed as a letter (A27, A34) and summarized by wire (A3, A5, A2); the correspondent saw the body, but no independent second account was found.

conflicts.note: The Lancaster letter is the best evidence: its writer reached the body early on Aug. 9. The Aug. 9 versions look like re-datings of the Aug. 9 wire.
